what_it_does: When a large language model generates text, its attention mechanism must repeatedly look up previously computed keys and values (a growing memory table called the KV cache — think of it as the model's running notes about everything said so far) stored in DRAM (the main memory chip). This is a memory-bandwidth problem: the processor spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from DRAM rather than actually doing math. One solution is processing-in-memory (PIM) — putting simple arithmetic circuits directly inside the DRAM chip so data never has to travel to the processor. AttenPIM applies this idea specifically to attention, but observes that attention involves two distinct kinds of vector-matrix multiply (a multiply where one input is a single row or column): the score computation (comparing the current query against stored keys) and the context computation (weighting stored values by those scores). These two operations have different shapes that change with the number of tokens in the conversation, so a one-size-fits-all PIM design wastes resources. AttenPIM instead uses a dual-mode PIM design where the in-memory arithmetic units can be reconfigured for whichever of the two operations is running, and stores the keys and values in a layout optimized for in-memory access patterns.
